reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes unusually high cryptocurrency returns and instructs viewers to deposit at least 0.2 ETH into a contract and activate an automated sandwich-trading bot. The speaker presents reported earnings of multiple ETH as a practical way to generate substantial income, while acknowledging fluctuating profits and possible gas-fee waste. The contract’s operation, reported returns, and recoverability of deposited funds are not verified.

citations.quote: How to Make +55% Profit Per Day with an Ethereum MEV Bot
Today I'll be teaching you step by step how to deploy an Ethereum trading bot
So the next step is to fund a contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
the more. You put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit. You'll be able to accumulate over time.
Last step is to click start.

opening.argument: Judge, the profit headline should be read alongside the speaker's qualifications. He says, "The profits will fluctuate week to week," rather than promising the same result every day. He also warns that a poorly funded contract can waste gas fees when it encounters high-burn-fee tokens. Those warnings do not prove the bot works, but they matter when deciding whether the presentation asserts a risk-free, fixed return. The more defensible reading is a risky trading tutorial built around reported results, not an unconditional promise of income.

citations.quote: The profits will fluctuate week to week.
If you fund the contract with 0.2 ETH or less, and the bot targets another token with high burn fees, the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.
How to Make +55% Profit Per Day with an Ethereum MEV Bot

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening rightly notes the funding instruction, but its inference from that instruction to deception overlooks the stated cost risk: the description explicitly warns that gas fees can be wasted. Likewise, the claim that returns are unverified is a limit on what we can conclude, not verification that the reported returns are false. The speaker qualifies those returns as variable.

citations.quote: So the next step is to fund a contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.
The profits will fluctuate week to week.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A warning about gas costs does not resolve the central concern. The title advertises a daily return, while the instructions tell viewers to fund the contract and say larger deposits can accumulate more profit. Acknowledging fluctuating results does not verify the bot's operation or the claimed ability to withdraw funds.

citations.quote: How to Make +55% Profit Per Day with an Ethereum MEV Bot
the more. You put in, the larger the transactions you will be able to sandwich and the more profit. You'll be able to accumulate over time.
When you click withdraw the bot will exit the liquidity pool and. Return the total Ethereum you entered initially including the profit back to. Your wallet.

opening.argument: Judge, the video spends substantial time walking through a Solidity workflow. The speaker directs viewers to create a contract file, compile it with the matching compiler version, and deploy through an injected provider; he also describes how transaction ordering is supposed to produce slippage profit. That is concrete instructional content a viewer can examine, not merely an unexplained appeal to send money. The earnings claims deserve skepticism, but the presence of a technical walkthrough supports treating the primary format as a demonstration rather than treating every asserted result as established fact.

citations.quote: It takes advantage of decentralized finance platforms such. As Uniswap to sandwich transactions for arbitrage.
We're going to name it bot.sol. Next, if you look in the description, I've included a link to the bot's source code.
Under Compiler, select the 0.6.6 version so that it matches our contract.
Here you're going to want to select Injected Provider as the environment.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening cites deployment, funding, and activation, but those steps also fit the demonstrated workflow: the speaker explains compiling and deploying the contract before discussing funding it. His account of a higher-gas transaction and a following sell order supplies a proposed trading mechanism. That explanation does not prove successful trading, but the funding step alone does not establish that the demonstration is deceptive.

citations.quote: Now click on the compile bot.sol button and wait for the bot to compile. So now we're going to deploy this to our wallet.
So the next step is to fund a contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
This will allow us to process our order. First, then process a sell order right after, in the same block.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Technical steps do not make this merely educational. The tutorial culminates in telling viewers to fund the contract and click start, while the title advertises a daily profit and the speaker reports gaining over half his deposit in about a day. The explanation of how the bot is supposed to trade does not establish that the supplied contract performs those trades.

citations.quote: So the next step is to fund a contract with some Ethereum to snipe liquidity pools.
Last step is to click start.
How to Make +55% Profit Per Day with an Ethereum MEV Bot
it basically took me a day to gain over half my deposit. Back.

opening.argument: Judge, the instructions describe deployment through the viewer's wallet and a deposit to the resulting contract address, not a stated payment to the speaker. The speaker tells viewers to check the address on Etherscan and describes a withdrawal control. Those are claims about the workflow, not proof that the funds are recoverable; still, the supplied account does not show a request for wallet credentials or a payment to the creator. The reported profit may be exaggerated, but the evidence presented does not establish those particular diversion mechanisms.

citations.quote: So now we're going to deploy this to our wallet.
Deposit funds (at least 0.2 ETH to prevent negating slippage) to your exact contract/bot address
I'm going to head back over to Etherscan and paste it in. Yep, it has created successfully.
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening's strongest point is that viewers are told to fund a contract. But the description calls it "your exact contract/bot address," and the speaker describes deploying through the viewer's wallet. The opening does not identify evidence in the supplied account that the address belongs to the creator or that a withdrawal fails. Those gaps do not verify the bot; they limit the conclusion drawn from the funding instruction alone.

citations.quote: to your exact contract/bot address
So now we're going to deploy this to our wallet.
Withdraw stops the bot and transfers the funds back into your wallet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A contract deployed through a viewer's wallet is not thereby shown to be safe. The instructions direct viewers to paste externally linked code, deposit at least 0.2 ETH into the contract, and activate it. Calling the address "your" contract and describing a withdrawal button do not establish what that code actually does or whether deposited funds can be recovered.
